title: Home equity can enable longer-lived and more varied entrepreneurship, but only for a small share of entry
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 21458; U.S. Census Bureau data on entrepreneurship and a 1998 Texas reform allowing home-equity lending
geography: United States local entrepreneurship, 1992–2007, with a Texas home-equity-lending reform case

observations.period: U.S. house prices, home equity, and entrepreneurship 1992–2007; paper issued 2015

denominator.unit: U.S. Census entrepreneurship and quasi-experimental home-equity study

house_price_entry.value: house-price growth was strongly correlated with local entrepreneurship

entry_composition.value: most entry associated with house-price growth was in construction and real estate, and those entrants tended to be small and short-lived

collateral_channel.value: entrepreneurship enabled through collateral after the 1998 Texas home-equity reform tended to be longer-lived and more balanced across sectors

collateral_share.value: the collateral channel represented a tenth or less of the entry associated with house-price increases and was driven by a small share of homeowners constrained without price growth

observations.method: The authors combine Census Bureau data on local entrepreneurship with a 1998 Texas reform that allowed home-equity lending for the first time in the state to isolate a collateral channel from broader house-price growth.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not follow each entrepreneur's household resources, local customers, jobs, wages, service, profits, ownership residence, or community outcomes. House-price correlation is not by itself causal, and the Texas reform does not represent every state, period, housing market, or borrower.
observations.subgroup: U.S. local entrants and homeowners, with the collateral-channel analysis centered on the Texas 1998 home-equity reform; effects may differ by homeowner liquidity, sector, place, housing market, and access to credit.
observations.counterinterpretation: Longer-lived or more sector-balanced entry does not establish good jobs, local service, durable community capacity, or household welfare. Home-equity borrowing can help a viable firm and expose a household to housing risk. Small short-lived entry may still provide experimentation or temporary work, while the paper does not identify its full social value.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 21458

boundary: This record adds a housing-collateral-to-entrepreneurship finding: home equity can enable longer-lived and more sector-balanced business entry, but the identified collateral channel is a small share of overall house-price-associated entry. It does not establish local ownership, customer benefit, job quality, durable survival, or household safety.
